author: Tertullian
addressee: Fabius, a brother in the faith
occasion: Fabius has asked whether Christians should flee during persecution. Tertullian writes to give a full answer, prompted both by Fabius's question and by the increasing frequency of persecutions.
argument: Tertullian argues that persecution comes from God, not ultimately from the devil, because God uses it to test and prove faith. Since persecution is God's will and is good, it should neither be avoided nor can it be escaped; fleeing is therefore wrong. The command to flee from city to city was given only to the apostles for a limited time and purpose, and no longer applies. Church leaders especially must not flee, and Christians must not buy their way out of persecution, since Christ has already purchased them with his blood. Those who truly have the Holy Spirit will neither flee nor pay to escape.

outline.move: Tertullian introduces Fabius's question and argues that persecution comes from God as a means of testing and proving faith.
He explains that although the devil's wickedness is involved, it serves only as God's instrument, and the devil has no power over God's servants without permission.
He cites Scripture to show that God brings both peace and war, wounding and healing, and that persecution is part of God's testing.
He concludes that since persecution is from God and is good, it must not be avoided and cannot be escaped.
He answers the objection that one may flee to avoid denying the faith, arguing that this shows distrust of God's protection.
He argues that the command to flee from city to city was temporary and applied only to the apostles before their mission to Israel was complete.
He shows that other sayings of the Lord about confessing him and enduring to the end contradict a permanent command to flee.

He explains that Christ's own withdrawal was temporary and for completing his teaching, and that Christ's prayer about the cup was made while standing firm, not while fleeing; believers may pray for relief only if they likewise stand and submit to the Father's will.
He argues that the apostles and the Spirit consistently exhort believers to endurance and martyrdom, not flight.
He rebukes those who use a pagan proverb to justify flight, urging Christians to stand as good soldiers of Christ.
He insists that church leaders especially must not flee, since the shepherd is bound to lay down his life for the sheep.
He argues that if flight is forbidden, buying oneself out of persecution is equally forbidden, since Christ has already purchased believers with his blood.

He answers objections from Scripture about giving to those who ask and making friends by means of money, and fiercely condemns churches that pay tribute to informers, comparing them to prostitutes and criminals.
He concludes with practical counsel on gathering for worship and a final exhortation to receive the Holy Spirit, who enables endurance.

cast.name: Fabius
cast.who: The brother who asked Tertullian whether one should flee in persecution.

cast.name: Rutilius
cast.who: A martyr who repeatedly fled and paid to avoid danger, yet was still arrested and killed.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle, cited as an example of one who refused to flee from suffering.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: The apostle, mentioned in connection with Christ's rebuke of his sword and Satan's request to sift him.

cast.name: John
cast.who: The apostle and author of Revelation, cited on laying down one's life and on fear.

cast.name: Moses
cast.who: Cited as an example of a shepherd willing to perish with his people.

cast.name: Job
cast.who: Cited as an example of one whom Satan could not tempt without God's permission.

cast.name: Saul
cast.who: King Saul, cited as an example of one handed over to an evil spirit for reprobation.

cast.name: Simon
cast.who: Simon Magus, who tried to buy the Spirit with money and was rebuked by Peter.

cast.name: Onesiphorus
cast.who: A believer mentioned as one who helped Paul, but not by paying money.

cast.who: A believer mentioned as one who helped Paul, but not by paying money.

key_terms.sense: The suffering and legal harassment inflicted on Christians for their faith, understood as God's testing
God's testing of faith through persecution, resulting in approval or rejection
God's rejection of those who fail the test of persecution
Flight from persecution, which Tertullian argues is forbidden
Paying money to escape persecution, which Tertullian equates with flight
Bearing witness to Christ through suffering and death
Denying Christ under pressure, including by avoiding confession
The Holy Spirit, the Comforter and guide into all truth, who enables endurance
Fearfulness that leads to flight or bribery, condemned as incompatible with love
Church leader responsible for the flock, who must not flee
The Christian congregation entrusted to its leaders
Wealth or money, especially as a rival master to God
An extortionist or informer who threatens Christians to extract money
Being handed over to the authorities by an informer

scripture: Tertullian uses Old Latin biblical texts, generally following Septuagint book names and Psalm numbering. He refers to 'Genesis' for Genesis, 'Apocalypsis' for Revelation, and cites prophets by their Septuagint names (e.g., Zacharias, Ezechiel, Hieremias). Modern citations should use standard English Bible names and numbering: Genesis, Revelation, Zechariah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, and the Psalms according to the Hebrew numbering used in most modern English Bibles.
uncertain: The exact date of composition; it is placed in Tertullian's Montanist period, but the precise year is debated.
The identity of Fabius beyond being a Christian brother.
Whether the 'quidam' who argued from the command to flee refers to a specific known individual.
The precise wording of some Old Latin biblical quotations, which vary among manuscripts.
The exact identity of the 'Rutilius' mentioned as a martyr.
